summary: The user was right and I was wrong: resources CAN be auto-provisioned at deploy time. I had asserted that D1 must be created beforehand and that database_id is required. Behaviour differs by path: wrangler dev creates local resources that persist; wrangler deploy creates them and writes their ids back to the config file; but deploying from the dashboard (which is what Workers Builds does) creates the resources and does NOT write the ids back into the repository. wrangler.jsonc was rewritten accordingly to omit database_id and bucket_name. Credential architecture specified by the user: only the key lives in the deployment secret, while each host address, port and credential is encrypted with that key and stored in D1, and arbitrary hosts plus their collection directory paths are added through the project front end. Implemented as: single SSH_MASTER_KEY secret; AES-GCM 256 via WebCrypto with a fresh random IV per encryption and the host id plus field name bound in as additional authenticated data; the API returns only a fingerprint, never a credential; hosts and source_rules tables added; global rules use a NULL host_id and per-host rules a host_id, unioned at collection time with exclusions evaluated first. Recorded as D32 and D33. An explicit honest limit is recorded rather than glossed over: an attacker holding both the D1 database and the master key can recover every credential.

summary: Prototype verdict: PASS. A deployed Worker connected to a real remote host over SSH and returned its bytes intact. Measured on the deployed Worker: ssh connect + auth 288-294 ms, sftp list /etc 202 ms (83 entries), sftp readFile 214 ms, WebCrypto sha256 under 1 ms, r2 put 217 ms; roughly 1.4 s end to end per file. Three files were checked against a hash computed independently ON THE HOST by sha256sum: /etc/hostname (24 bytes), /etc/alpine-release (7 bytes) and /etc/passwd (1226 bytes) all matched exactly, and the R2 objects were confirmed present with identical sizes. This closes the CPU-budget risk recorded as D24: the handshake uses about one hundredth of the paid plan ceiling, so the collection channel chosen in D14 is viable.

Bug found only against a real host, and the reason it could not be caught locally: Wrangler bundles without type checking, and edgeport AlgorithmPrefs.cipher is an ARRAY of algorithm names, but the code passed a bare string. The handshake therefore died at KEXINIT construction with TypeError names.join is not a function. Fixed by passing a preference list with AES-GCM first and aes-ctr as fallback; chacha20-poly1305 stays excluded because it would be pure JS. A list was chosen over a single pinned cipher so a host without GCM still works. The JSON error response now also carries a stack, because with no type checking in the build a dependency shape mistake can only surface at runtime and a stack turns that from guesswork into a line number.

summary: Scale limits supplied by the user, answering Q7 and closing it: at most 50 devices (hosts), no single file larger than 100 MB, and total R2 usage must stay at or below 10 GB. The 100 MB per-file figure agrees with what event e014 already recorded ("single-file maximum size generally under 100 MB"), so that part is a confirmation rather than a change. The 10 GB ceiling is NEW and is a CAPACITY BUDGET, not merely a size limit: it implies the store must bound its own total bytes, which in turn requires a retention/eviction policy and a decision about whether superseded object versions stay in R2. Nothing in the schema or the code measures or enforces total stored bytes today. The 50-host figure bounds a full sweep and therefore the run/resume design, because D13 caps a single Cron invocation at 15 minutes of wall clock.

Grill round 4 answers. Q1 ACCEPTED: a cron sweep that works within a wall-clock budget and persists a cursor (which host, which path) into D1, resuming on the next invocation, with a target freshness of 15-30 minutes. Q2 REVISED BY THE USER, overriding the recommendation: old files are to be deleted automatically to stay inside the 10 GB budget, but files carrying an IMPORTANT mark are never deleted, and if the important-marked set alone fills the budget then no new files are synchronised at all. This introduces a requirement that did not exist before - a per-object importance/pin flag plus an eviction policy that must never delete a pinned object, and a capacity guard that refuses new work rather than evicting pins. Note the old policy of never deleting anything is now explicitly rejected. Q4 ACCEPTED: two tables, collection_runs plus collection_issues, to hold receipts including capacity refusals, which only become visible if they are persisted. Q3 PARTIALLY ANSWERED BUT CONFLICTS WITH A VERIFIED PLATFORM FACT: the user asked for a custom domain to serve presigned downloads with a 2-hour expiry and an optional share password, and D11 (research section 9.2, citing https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/) states that presigned URLs work only on <ACCOUNT_ID>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com and CANNOT be used with custom domains, the documented alternative being a public bucket behind WAF HMAC validation (Pro plan or above). The requirement as stated is achievable, but only by the Worker issuing its own short-lived signed token and streaming the object, not by an R2 presigned URL. That reinterpretation is PROPOSED, not yet confirmed by the user. Also recorded: the user pasted a root password into the conversation for the test host (identified dashboard-side, deliberately not written here); the repository is public, so the credential is deliberately NOT written anywhere in the repository and should be rotated after the experiment.

D28 was half wrong and is corrected. It asserted that Cloudflare provides NO CLI or API path for connecting a repository to a Worker, so the connection had to be a human-only dashboard step. That is false: Cloudflare documents a Workers Builds REST API (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/api-reference/, updated 2026-09-22) whose from-scratch example creates the repository connection (PUT /accounts/{id}/builds/repos/connections) and the production and preview triggers (POST /accounts/{id}/builds/triggers) entirely by API. What remains genuinely human-only is narrower and different: the one-time installation and authorization of the Cloudflare GitHub App, which requires an OAuth grant on the GitHub side. The documentation states this explicitly - once that one-time setup is done, the API can do everything else. Credential requirement, measured rather than assumed: the API needs a USER-scoped API token with the Workers Builds Configuration: Edit permission, and the existing wrangler OAuth token is NOT sufficient - GET /accounts/{id}/builds/tokens and GET /builds/repos/connections both returned 403 code 10000 Authentication error on 2026-10-07, while GET /accounts/{id}/workers/scripts succeeded with the same token, which isolates the failure to the Builds permission rather than to authentication in general. Recorded so no future session repeats the claim that the dashboard is the only path, and so the real prerequisite (GitHub App authorization) is not confused with the one that was wrongly claimed.

summary: Q4 is closed and D44 is confirmed by the user. The download mechanism is a Worker-issued short-lived token plus a streamed R2 body, NOT an R2 presigned URL, because a presigned URL cannot be used with a custom domain (verified in D11 / research section 9.2). The user wants a custom domain, a two-hour validity window, and an optional password share. A Worker-issued token delivers all three and is strictly better than presigning on two counts: it is revocable, whereas a presigned URL is an irrevocable bearer token, and it can actually enforce the download-time password check from D15, which a presigned URL bypasses entirely because R2 knows nothing about the password. The accepted cost is that downloads consume this Worker's concurrency and wall-clock budget.
